newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: In N.Korea tension heralds diplomatic initiative.
newsitem.headline: In N.Korea tension heralds diplomatic initiative.

text.p: A visit to Pyongyang by two U.S. emissaries underscored North Korea's desire to emerge from isolation despite recent border brinkmanship, North Korea watchers in Seoul said on Wednesday.

The visit by former senator Sam Nunn and former ambassador to South Korea James Laney also highlighted the dire economic problems that are pushing the reclusive state into crucial four-nation peace talks, they said.

"There were two main themes North Korea was focusing on during their visit. One is food and economic assistance and the other is a goal to forge better ties with the U.S.," said Park Sung-hoon, senior analyst at Seoul's unification ministry.

Nunn, who once headed the Senate Armed Services Committee and is a respected American voice on national security issues, and Laney, an expert on North Korea, went to Pyongyang on a fact-finding mission ahead of the four-nation talks.

Senior officials from the two Koreas, the United States and China are due to meet in New York on August 5 to pave the way for talks aimed at hammering out a permanent peace settlement on the Korean peninsula.
Park said the most significant meeting Nunn and Laney had in Pyongyang was with Lieutenant General Ri Chan-bok, chief of the Korean People's Army Panmunjom Mission.

The mission at the border village of Panmunjom was set up in 1994 as part of Pyongyang's campaign to press the United States to sign a bilateral peace treaty to replace the now fraying 1953 armistice that ended the three-year Korean War.

"Although the North agreed to discuss peace in four-nation talks, it was maintaining that any peace arrangement on the Korean peninsula must be primarily worked out between Pyongyang and Washington," Park said.
Many Seoul-based experts on North Korea said they believed a border clash last week was engineered by Pyongyang to stress the need to set up a communications channel with the U.S. military.
"The North was heightening border tensions ahead of the visit by U.S. heavyweights," said Yu Suk-ryul, a fellow at state-funded Institute of Foreign Affairs and National Security.

A fierce exchange of fire at the Demilitarized Zone followed an intrusion by North Korean soldiers across the demarcation line bisecting the DMZ. The North said several of its soldiers were wounded in the exchange of fire, which involved heavy weaponry.
The North, which calls South Korea a "U.S. puppet", has refused to discuss border incidents with the South, insisting that U.S. and North Korean generals should address such issues.
"North Korean leadership bases its existence on combating enemy South Korea," Yu said. "All it wants from four-nation talks is food, economic aid and better ties with the U.S."

Nunn, in a Seoul news conference on Tuesday after a two-day visit to the North, said he and Laney discussed with the North Korean general the need to reduce tensions along the Korean border, the last Cold War flashpoint.

Nunn said the general "had a different view on many aspects" but "one thing that we did agree on is that we do need to find ways to improve communications. There is no question that the lack of communications is a danger in an area of risk".
He said Pyongyang officials stressed the need for more food aid and asked for the removal of U.S. economic sanctions and for increased economic cooperation.
Lee Jong-seok, fellow at the Sejong Institute, a private think-tank, said the North saw better ties with Washington and Tokyo as an exit from economic ruin.
"Pyongyang will seek more than $5 billion as a compensation for Japan's colonial rule of Korea when it normalises ties with Tokyo," Lee said.
"I think four-party talks will not lead to an immediate breakthrough but they will continue as it seems that the North is viewing four-party talks as an important survival card."
